title: The thirteen principles
hookLine: his list of core Jewish beliefs, in his commentary on Sanhedrin 10

lines: A SHARE IN THE WORLD TO COME.
THE MISHNAH DOESN'T SAY WHAT IT IS.
cards: All Israel have a share in the world to come. That, in paraphrase, is how a chapter of the Mishnah, in tractate Sanhedrin, opens. It backs the line with a verse from Isaiah: "Thy people also shall be all righteous."
Then it names a few people who lose that share. The Mishnah stops there. It doesn't say what a share is, or what a person has to hold to keep one.
Maimonides, working through the Mishnah passage by passage, reaches this chapter and decides the question can't wait. So he writes an answer, and the answer becomes a list.

teach.b: The thirteen principles. First, what he called them. Not commandments and not rules.
In the Hebrew translation, they are yesodot, foundations, the stones a house stands on. You don't live in the foundation. You live in the house.
But without it, the house doesn't stand. Second, the shape of the list.

teach.h: THREE STRETCHES: GOD, TORAH, WHAT'S TO COME.
teach.b: It moves in three stretches. The first five are about God. The next four are about prophecy and the Torah.
The last four are about what God knows and does, and what is still to come. Over the next three days, we'll take one stretch a day. Third, why it was new.
The Torah gives commandments. The Mishnah gives laws and arguments.

Neither one stops to hand you a numbered list of beliefs. Maimonides did, in the middle of a commentary on the oral law, because he thought a person ought to know what the foundations are, not only what to do.
Later, his list was set in verse and printed in prayer books, and it was also questioned. Other scholars drew up lists of their own. That argument has a day of its own later this week.
For now, notice the move. Faced with a single word in an old text, a share, Maimonides asked what it rests on, and wrote it down so that anyone could read it.

how: Maimonides' thirteen principles are studied in his commentary on Sanhedrin, and versions of them appear in prayer books, both as the poem Yigdal and as a series of lines that each begin "I believe with complete faith."

games.q: you're Maimonides. the Mishnah says all Israel have a share in the world to come, but never says what that share rests on. what do you do?
o: explain the words and move on.
write out the foundations a person should know.
games.why: he stops and sets out thirteen foundations, in the middle of a commentary on law.

practice: Here is the list, plainly: God exists; God is one; God has no body; God is eternal; only God is to be worshiped; the prophets spoke truth; the prophecy of Moses stands apart; the Torah is from heaven; the Torah will not be replaced; God knows what people do; God rewards and punishes; the messiah will come; the dead will live.
Hear it once without sorting it, and notice which line stays with you.
